title: Organizing Yourself Relationally
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Field Note describes an alternative to the typical task-and-calendar-driven approach to productivity: organizing one's schedule primarily around people rather than to-do items. Leaders who work this way maintain a running list of relationships that matter -- mentors, peers, family, team members -- and schedule time to check in before deciding what tasks to tackle, often aiming to never let a meaningful relationship go more than roughly 90 days without contact. The piece presents this as a deliberate philosophy for leaders who believe long-term success flows primarily from the strength and breadth of their relationships.
points: An alternative productivity model organizes daily and weekly time around people rather than tasks.
Practitioners keep an ongoing, curated list of relationships that matter and update it continuously.
A rough benchmark is offered: never go more than 90 days without meaningfully connecting with people on the list.
This method requires maintaining the relationship list externally, since it's too large to track mentally.
The piece frames this as a deliberate philosophy for leaders who see relationships as the core driver of success.
quotes: When leaders think of being highly effective, efficient, and organized, they naturally turn to thoughts of strategy, tasks, and tactics that promote productivity.
Yet, many of the world’s best leaders operate on a track they believe is better than organizing themselves around tasks, processes, and meetings. These leaders organize themselves relationally.
Essentially, leaders who organize themselves relationally replace to-dos or tasks with people.
Maintaining this list is essential, as no one can do this in their head for more than a few dozen relationships.
Relationally organized leaders try never to go more than 90 days without conversing with those they don’t engage with naturally through their work or family life.
